title: Acids, bases and pH
blurb: Define acids and bases, use the logarithmic pH scale, tell strong from concentrated and explain how buffers hold blood pH between 7.35 and 7.45.
question: Gastric juice has a pH of about 2 and a cola about 3, while blood sits between 7.35 and 7.45. How much more acidic is gastric juice than cola, and what keeps blood pH so steady?

teach.h: What makes an acid or a base
teach.body: Arrhenius: an acid produces H⁺ (as hydronium, H₃O⁺) in water; a base produces OH⁻ (hydroxide). Brønsted-Lowry: an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor and a base is a proton acceptor, so NH₃ counts as a base even without OH⁻. In plain English: acids hand off H⁺, bases catch it. In HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of HCl. (Lewis: acids accept, bases donate electron pairs.)

pH = −log[H⁺]. The scale usually runs 0 to 14, with 7 neutral (pure water at 25 °C, where [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ M). Lower pH means more H⁺, so a more acidic solution. Each 1 pH unit is a 10-fold change in [H⁺]: pH 3 is 10 times more acidic than pH 4 and 100 times more than pH 5. Also, pH + pOH = 14.

teach.caption: Stomach acid 1.5–3.5, urine about 6, milk 6.5, seawater 8, baking soda 8–9, bleach 12–13, lye 14.

teach.h: One pH step = 10 times the H⁺
teach.caption: Three pH units apart means 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 times the hydrogen ion concentration, not 3 times.

head: Strong (ionize fully)
Weak (ionize partly)
rows: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₄
teach.caption: 'Strong' describes how completely an acid ionizes, not how concentrated it is. A dilute strong acid is still strong; a concentrated weak acid is still weak.

teach.body: Acid + base → salt + water (HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O); antacids neutralize stomach acid. In a titration, a base of known concentration is added to an acid (or the reverse) with an indicator to find the unknown concentration. A buffer resists pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added; it is usually a weak acid plus its conjugate base. Blood's main buffer is carbonic acid / bicarbonate (H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻).

teach.h: How the body defends blood pH

steps.label: Kidneys
steps.sub: Adjust H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ (hours to days)

teach.caption: Blood pH below 7.35 is acidosis; above 7.45 is alkalosis.

teach.body: Sofia, a nursing applicant, compares gastric juice (pH 2), a cola (pH 3) and blood (pH 7.4). Gastric juice is one pH unit lower than cola, so it has 10 times the H⁺. Blood is slightly basic. An antacid such as Mg(OH)₂ neutralizes stomach acid: Mg(OH)₂ + 2 HCl → MgCl₂ + 2 H₂O, a salt plus water.

teach.text: pH 3 is 1,000 times (not 3 times) more acidic than pH 6. LOWER pH is more acidic. Acids turn BLUE litmus RED. Bases ACCEPT protons. Strong does not mean concentrated, and acetic and carbonic acids are weak. Blood is slightly BASIC. A buffer resists change; it does not hold pH exactly constant. pH + pOH = 14, not 7.

items: Acid: H⁺ donor (makes H₃O⁺ in water). Base: H⁺ acceptor (or makes OH⁻).
Acids: sour, blue litmus → red, pH < 7. Bases: bitter, slippery, red litmus → blue, phenolphthalein pink, pH > 7.
pH is logarithmic: each unit is a 10-fold change in [H⁺]; pH + pOH = 14.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; strength is not concentration.
Acid + base → salt + water. Buffers resist pH change; blood uses H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻ to stay at 7.35–7.45.

summary: You can now define acids and bases two ways, identify conjugate pairs and predict indicator colors. You can also compare solutions on the logarithmic pH scale, separate strength from concentration, write a neutralization and explain how the bicarbonate buffer, lungs and kidneys hold blood at pH 7.35 to 7.45.

A.q: A solution turns blue litmus paper red. Which pH is it most likely to have?
A.why: Acids turn blue litmus red, and acids have a pH below 7.

whyNot.0: pH 7 is neutral and would not change litmus color.
whyNot.2: pH 9 is basic; a base turns red litmus blue.
whyNot.3: pH 12 is strongly basic; it would turn red litmus blue.

A.q: Under the Brønsted-Lowry definition, a base is a:
A.why: Brønsted-Lowry bases accept protons (H⁺); acids donate them.

whyNot.0: Donating protons defines a Brønsted-Lowry acid.
whyNot.1: An electron-pair acceptor is a Lewis ACID.
whyNot.3: Producing hydronium (H₃O⁺) in water describes an Arrhenius acid.

A.q: How many times greater is the hydrogen ion concentration at pH 3 than at pH 6?
A.why: Each pH unit is a factor of 10. A 3-unit difference: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000.

whyNot.1: pH is logarithmic, not linear; 3 units is not 3 times.
whyNot.2: 30 multiplies the difference by 10 instead of raising 10 to the power 3.
whyNot.3: 10,000 would be a 4-unit difference (for example pH 2 vs pH 6).

B.q: Which of these is a strong acid?
B.why: Nitric acid ionizes completely in water, so it is one of the strong acids.

whyNot.0: Acetic acid (vinegar) ionizes only partially: a weak acid.
whyNot.1: Carbonic acid (in soda and blood) is a weak acid.
whyNot.2: Despite fluorine's reactivity, HF ionizes only partially and is a weak acid.

B.q: Which describes normal human blood pH?
B.why: Normal blood pH is 7.35–7.45, just above 7, so it is slightly basic.

whyNot.1: 6.35–6.45 would be acidic and far outside the normal range.
whyNot.2: Blood is kept slightly above neutral, not at exactly 7.
whyNot.3: The range is right, but any pH above 7 is basic, not acidic.

B.q: What are the products when hydrochloric acid is neutralized by sodium hydroxide?
B.why: Acid + base → salt + water: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.

whyNot.0: Hydrogen gas forms when an acid reacts with an active metal, not with a base.
whyNot.1: Chlorine stays as chloride in the salt; no Cl₂ gas is released.
whyNot.3: NaOCl (bleach) and H₂ are not products of neutralization, which always gives a salt plus water.

C.q: In the reaction HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, what is the conjugate base of HCl?
C.why: HCl donates a proton; what remains, Cl⁻, is its conjugate base.

whyNot.0: H₂O is the base that accepts the proton, not the conjugate base of HCl.
whyNot.1: H₃O⁺ is the conjugate ACID of water.
whyNot.3: OH⁻ does not appear in this reaction.

C.q: A student says, 'A very dilute solution of HCl is a weak acid.' Which response is correct?
options: Yes; dilute acids are weak acids
Yes; HCl ionizes partly when dilute
No; 'weak' acids have a pH above 7
C.why: Strength describes the degree of ionization. HCl ionizes completely at any concentration, so a dilute HCl solution is a dilute STRONG acid.

whyNot.0: This confuses strength with concentration; dilute is not the same as weak.
whyNot.1: HCl ionizes fully regardless of how dilute the solution is.
whyNot.2: Weak acids still have a pH below 7; they just ionize only partly.

C.q: A small amount of acid is added to a blood sample containing the bicarbonate buffer. What happens to the pH?
options: It falls as much as in water
C.why: HCO₃⁻ binds most of the added H⁺, forming H₂CO₃, so pH drops only a little: the buffer resists change.

whyNot.0: Buffers resist change; they do not keep pH perfectly constant.
whyNot.2: Adding acid cannot raise the pH; it adds H⁺.
whyNot.3: Unbuffered water would show a large drop; the buffer prevents that.

reteach.title: Counting the zeros
reteach.question: If one jar holds 0.001 g of a substance and another holds 0.0001 g, which holds more, and how many times more? That is exactly how the pH scale works.

blocks.h: pH is a count of decimal places
blocks.body: The pH number tells you where the hydrogen ion concentration's decimal point sits: pH 3 means [H⁺] = 0.001 M, pH 4 means 0.0001 M. One extra zero is ten times less. So a bigger pH number means FEWER hydrogen ions, which is why low pH is acidic. Moving 3 places is like going from $1,000 to $1: a 1,000-fold change, not 3-fold.

blocks.text: Subtract the pH values, then raise 10 to that power. pH 2 vs pH 5: difference 3, so 10³ = 1,000 times.

explain.body: Acids donate H⁺ (sour; blue litmus turns red; react with metals to give H₂). Bases accept H⁺ or make OH⁻ (bitter, slippery; red litmus turns blue; phenolphthalein pink).

test.q: Which property belongs to a base?
test.why: Bases turn red litmus paper blue (and phenolphthalein pink).

whyNot.1: Turning blue litmus red is an acid property.
whyNot.2: A sour taste is typical of acids; bases taste bitter.
whyNot.3: Releasing hydrogen gas with active metals is an acid property.

explain.body: pH = −log[H⁺]; 7 is neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 basic. Each unit is a 10-fold change. pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C.

test.q: A solution at 25 °C has a pOH of 4. What is its pH?
test.why: pH + pOH = 14, so pH = 14 − 4 = 10 (a basic solution).

whyNot.0: pH and pOH are equal only at 7 (neutral).
whyNot.1: 7 is neutral; a pOH of 4 means the solution is basic.
whyNot.2: 18 adds the pOH to 14; the pOH must be subtracted: 14 − 4.

explain.body: Strong acids and bases ionize completely; weak ones only partly. Strong bases: group 1 hydroxides and some group 2 (Ca(OH)₂, Ba(OH)₂). Weak bases: ammonia, bicarbonate. Strength is not concentration.

test.q: Which of these is a weak base?
test.why: Ammonia (NH₃) accepts protons from water but reacts only partly, so it is a weak base.

whyNot.0: NaOH is a group 1 hydroxide: a strong base.
whyNot.2: KOH is a group 1 hydroxide: a strong base.
whyNot.3: Ca(OH)₂ is one of the group 2 hydroxides classed as strong bases.

explain.body: Acid + base → salt + water. A buffer (weak acid + its conjugate base) resists pH change. In blood, H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻ buffers; the lungs adjust CO₂ in minutes and the kidneys adjust H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ over hours to days.

test.q: What is the main buffer system in human blood?
test.why: Blood's main buffer is carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) with its conjugate base bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻).

whyNot.0: Sulfuric acid is a strong acid, and a buffer needs a weak acid; it is not the blood buffer.
whyNot.1: HCl is a strong acid (found in the stomach), so it cannot form a buffer pair.
whyNot.3: Acetic acid / acetate can make a buffer in the lab, but it is not the body's blood buffer.
